segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Phoebe Langton went up the staircase of Amberlight House with the three guineas still shut in her fist, and did not think once about whether she had been asked in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the landing a travelling trunk lay over on its side, and a great many letters had gone across the boards with it, some tied in bundles and some loose. A jet bead was still rolling when she came up. Miss Fairfax lay beside the trunk with her eyes shut, and Harker knelt at her head with his coat off and folded under it.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: She was carrying it down. The handle came away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was nothing left in his voice of the man who had stood in the hall on Thursday and told her that her business was the cloth.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: Open that window and go down for water. I have brought three sisters round off a hot kitchen floor and I know how it is done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went. Phoebe knelt and chafed the girl's hands, and by the time he was back on the landing with a cup, Miss Fairfax had got her eyes open and was looking at the ceiling.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: I am very sorry. I am always sorry. It is all I seem to say.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She sat up against the wall and saw the letters over the boards, and her hands began gathering them without her appearing to know it.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: You are the dressmaker. You came for my measure and he would not let you have it.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: Then you may as well have the rest. I was to be married in June. Old Sir Edward left me four hundred pounds, and I had met him twice, and his lawyers were a twelvemonth about it. When the sum was known, his mother said in a room with nine people in it that I had gone after a dead man's money and would next go after a living one's. In April it was ended. I came away where no one has seen my face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Phoebe set the cup down on the boards.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: And that is the whole of it.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: That is the whole of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Harker had got up and stood with his back to the window.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: Your account at the draper's was one pound eleven. I sent a man down with it on Friday.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: I know what you sent. I came to give it back.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: I had used you badly and I knew it before you were off the step. I would not put my name to it because this house has been shut six years, and the first kindness that comes out of it with a name on it will set the parish asking what else is in here. I would rather be thought mean.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: You are thought a great deal worse than mean, sir.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had got no further than that when they all three heard it. A voice came up the staircase out of the hall below, warm and perfectly sure of itself, and a second voice under it agreeing.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: The door is standing open, Mrs Hale. I have said these three days that something would come of those lights, and the door is standing open.
